name: Java SE, Jakarta EE, and Java ME
overview: Three Java editions walk into an interview. Pick the right one for a desktop tool, a web service, or a small device, and explain why.

sections.title: Java SE for general-purpose programs
sections.content: Java SE is the base platform. It includes the language, JVM, and standard APIs you use for files, networking, concurrency, and more.

sections.title: Jakarta EE for enterprise APIs
sections.content: Jakarta EE adds standards such as Servlet and Persistence. Jakarta EE 8 kept the older javax packages. Jakarta EE 9 moved its enterprise APIs to jakarta packages.

sections.title: Java ME for constrained devices
sections.content: Java ME targets devices with limited resources and a compatible runtime. Choose it by checking the target device and the APIs the application needs.

images.caption: Choose according to the deployment target and APIs you need.

keyPoints: Assign each example to an edition and name one feature it needs. Bonus point for spotting when a migration needs new dependencies as well as new imports.

interviewQA.question: Which edition would you use for a standalone desktop tool?
interviewQA.answer: Start with Java SE. Add libraries for any capabilities your tool needs.

interviewQA.question: Did every javax package become jakarta?
interviewQA.answer: The Jakarta EE enterprise APIs changed. Java SE packages such as javax.sql kept their names.
